title: Sick-day rules, SGLT-2 safety and the diabetic foot
blurb: Teach which medicines to pause when someone is dehydrated, spot euglycaemic DKA on SGLT-2 inhibitors, and examine and refer the diabetic foot on time.
question: Mr Shah, 63, takes metformin, dapagliflozin and ramipril. He has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days and is drinking little. He phones the practice asking what to do with his tablets. What is the best advice?

teach.body: Sick-day rules are a written plan, agreed in advance, for what a person with diabetes does with their medicines when they are unwell, especially with vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration. NICE NG28 (2026) says every treatment plan should state which medicines to stop, how to adjust insulin, and, just as important, how to restart once recovered. Plain English: some tablets become risky when you are dry; insulin is adjusted, not abandoned.

teach.caption: The plan must also say how to restart; the NICE committee reported seeing medicines stopped but not started again.

teach.body: SGLT-2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin and others) can cause DKA in which glucose is near normal, so a reassuring meter reading can hide it. Before starting one, NICE asks you to check for previous DKA, intercurrent illness, dehydration risk, and very low-carbohydrate or ketogenic diets. If someone on an SGLT-2 inhibitor is unwell with nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain or breathlessness, check ketones, whatever the glucose.

steps.label: Escalate
steps.sub: Raised ketones: urgent assessment for DKA

teach.caption: Around surgery, JBDS 03 omits SGLT-2 inhibitors the day before and the day of surgery, with daily ketone checks while in hospital.

teach.text: 'His glucose is only 9, so it can't be DKA' is wrong on an SGLT-2 inhibitor. Euglycaemic DKA is diagnosed on ketones and acidosis, and 'known diabetes' satisfies the D criterion. Also, sick-day rules pause metformin and SGLT-2 inhibitors, but insulin is adjusted, never just stopped.

items: Examine both feet on any admission to hospital, and if their condition changes.
Remove shoes, socks, bandages and dressings first.
Look for neuropathy (10 g monofilament), ischaemia, ulceration, callus, infection, deformity, gangrene and Charcot arthropathy.
Give moderate and high-risk inpatients a pressure redistribution device to offload the heels.

bands.label: Previous ulcer/amputation, RRT, or combined factors
Ulcer, infection, CLTI, gangrene, suspected Charcot

teach.caption: An unexplained hot, swollen, discoloured foot (with or without pain) suggests acute Charcot: treat as active.

children.label: Refer immediately to acute services
children.sub: Ulcer with sepsis or ischaemia, deep infection, gangrene

teach.h: Scenario: Mrs Taylor admitted with pneumonia
teach.body: Mrs Taylor, 71, has type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy. On admission the nurse removes her socks and finds a small, sloughy ulcer on her left heel she had not noticed. She has no fever and the foot is warm with palpable pulses. The nurse documents it, offloads her heels with a pressure redistribution device, informs the team and makes sure she is referred to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 24 hours of that examination.

items: Every treatment plan has sick-day rules: what to stop, insulin changes, and how to restart.
Dehydration risk: pause metformin and SGLT-2 inhibitors; consider pausing ACE inhibitors/ARBs.
On an SGLT-2 inhibitor and unwell: check ketones even if glucose is normal.
Examine both feet, shoes and dressings off, on any hospital admission.
Limb- or life-threatening foot: refer immediately; inpatient foot problem: MDT within 24 hours.

summary: You can now give sick-day advice on which medicines to pause and how to restart them, and recognise euglycaemic DKA in someone taking an SGLT-2 inhibitor. You can also examine the diabetic foot on admission, stratify risk and refer within NICE NG19 time limits.

A.q: Mr Shah, 63, takes metformin, dapagliflozin and ramipril. He has had vomiting and diarrhoea for 2 days and is drinking little. Which advice best matches sick-day rules?
options: Double his metformin to control glucose
Continue all three with extra water
Stop all tablets and wait a week to restart
A.why: NICE NG28 rec 1.10.1: sick-day rules specify stopping medicines such as metformin and SGLT-2 inhibitors when there is risk of dehydration, vomiting and diarrhoea. NG148 rec 1.2.14: consider temporarily stopping ACE inhibitors and ARBs in diarrhoea, vomiting or sepsis.

whyNot.0: Increasing metformin while dehydrated adds risk and is not part of sick-day rules.
whyNot.2: Continuing these medicines while dehydrated raises the risk of AKI and DKA.
whyNot.3: Sick-day rules include a plan to restart once recovered, not an arbitrary week.

A.q: Mrs Ito takes empagliflozin. She has abdominal pain, nausea and fast breathing. Her capillary glucose is 9.4 mmol/L. What should the nurse check next?
A.why: SGLT-2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose (NG28 1.21; JBDS 02). Abdominal pain, nausea and rapid breathing need an urgent ketone check.

whyNot.0: HbA1c reflects 2–3 months of control and does not detect DKA now.
whyNot.1: Postural BP does not diagnose ketoacidosis.
whyNot.3: Nitrites screen for urinary infection, not ketoacidosis.

A.q: Mr Evans, 68, with type 2 diabetes, is admitted with heart failure. When should his feet be examined, according to NICE NG19?
options: On admission, with shoes and socks off
At his next annual diabetes review
If he reports pain in his feet
A.why: NICE NG19 recs 1.3.3–1.3.4: assess foot risk on any admission to hospital (and if status changes), removing shoes, socks, bandages and dressings and examining both feet.

whyNot.1: Annual review is for community care; admission triggers its own assessment.
whyNot.2: Neuropathy means problems may be painless, so assessment is routine, not symptom-led.
whyNot.3: Leaving it to discharge misses problems that need referral within 24 hours.

B.q: Mrs Taylor, an inpatient, has a new heel ulcer with no signs of infection or ischaemia. Within what time should she be referred to the multidisciplinary foot care service?
options: Within 24 hours of the foot exam
B.why: NICE NG19 rec 1.1.3: refer the person to the multidisciplinary foot care service within 24 hours of the initial examination of their feet.

whyNot.0: 2 weeks is far beyond the 24-hour inpatient standard.
whyNot.2: 6–8 weeks is the foot protection service assessment time for moderate risk in the community.
whyNot.3: Waiting until discharge delays care of an active ulcer.

B.q: Mr Patel has a foot ulcer and is now febrile and tachycardic, with spreading redness up his ankle. What is the correct action?
options: Refer to the foot protection service
Dress the ulcer and review in 48 hours
B.why: NICE NG19 rec 1.4.1: ulceration with fever or any signs of sepsis is limb- or life-threatening; refer immediately to acute services and inform the MDT foot service.

whyNot.0: The foot protection service manages risk, not a limb-threatening infection.
whyNot.1: 1 working day is for other active foot problems, not sepsis.
whyNot.2: Delay risks sepsis progression and limb loss.

B.q: During a foot check, which finding would place a person in the NG19 'high risk' category?
options: Callus with no other risk factor
B.why: NICE NG19 rec 1.3.6: previous ulceration (or amputation, renal replacement therapy, or combined factors) is high risk.

whyNot.0: Callus without other factors is low risk.
whyNot.1: Neuropathy without other factors is moderate risk.
whyNot.3: Deformity without other factors is moderate risk.

C.q: Mr Kowalski, 70, takes dapagliflozin and metformin and is admitted with a urinary tract infection. Glucose 11.2 mmol/L, ketones 3.8 mmol/L, venous pH 7.24. The doctor says DKA is unlikely because glucose is only mildly raised. What should the nurse do?
options: Accept the view and recheck glucose in 4 hours
Give his evening dapagliflozin as prescribed
Encourage oral fluids and repeat ketones tomorrow
Escalate, as the results meet DKA criteria
C.why: JBDS 02: DKA = known diabetes or glucose above 11.0, ketones above 3.0, and pH below 7.3 (or bicarbonate below 15). SGLT-2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose, so escalate using the results.

whyNot.0: Glucose is not the measure of DKA; ketones and pH are, and they meet the criteria.
whyNot.1: The SGLT-2 inhibitor should be withheld when unwell and ketotic.
whyNot.2: Delaying recognition of DKA is unsafe; he needs the DKA pathway now.

C.q: Mrs Green recovered from gastroenteritis a week ago. Her metformin and empagliflozin were paused while she was unwell and have not been restarted. She is eating and drinking normally. What does NICE emphasise here?
options: Leave them stopped until her next annual review
Sick-day plans should say how to restart
Restart metformin; stop empagliflozin for good
Wait for an HbA1c result before restarting
C.why: NICE NG28 rec 1.10.1 (2026): sick-day rules should state how to restart medication after recovery; the NICE committee reported seeing medicines stopped but not started again.

whyNot.0: Leaving them off until an annual review is exactly the gap NICE warns about.
whyNot.2: Illness alone is not a reason to stop the SGLT-2 inhibitor permanently.
whyNot.3: HbA1c changes slowly; restarting follows recovery, not a blood test.

C.q: Mr Ward, 76, has diabetes and peripheral neuropathy and is in hospital after a stroke, mostly in bed. His feet are intact. What foot care does NICE NG19 recommend while he is an inpatient?
options: A pressure redistribution device to offload his heels
Daily foot soaks in warm water
Elevate his heels on a single pillow under each
Weekly foot checks by the podiatrist
C.why: NICE NG19 rec 1.3.12: people in hospital at moderate or high risk of a diabetic foot problem should have a pressure redistribution device to offload heel pressure, and be referred to the foot protection service on discharge.

whyNot.1: Soaking macerates skin and risks burns with neuropathy; it is not NG19 advice.
whyNot.2: A pillow under each heel still loads the heels; NG19 specifies a pressure redistribution device.
whyNot.3: Weekly podiatry is not the inpatient standard; offloading and reassessment on status change are.

reteach.title: Dry days and hidden feet
reteach.question: Two things go wrong quietly in diabetes: medicines on dry days, and feet nobody looks at. What protects against each?

blocks.body: Dry days: when vomiting, diarrhoea or not drinking, pause metformin and SGLT-2 inhibitors (and consider pausing ACE inhibitors or ARBs), keep insulin going with adjusted doses, check ketones, and restart when well. Hidden feet: neuropathy hides pain, so on every admission take off shoes, socks and dressings and look. Anything threatening the limb or life goes to acute services now; other inpatient foot problems go to the MDT within 24 hours.

blocks.text: Near-normal glucose does not exclude DKA in someone taking an SGLT-2 inhibitor.

explain.body: Each plan states whether medicines change if unwell or having surgery, which to stop with dehydration, vomiting or diarrhoea (metformin, SGLT-2 inhibitors), how to adjust insulin, and how to restart after recovery.

test.q: Which medicine does NICE NG28 name as one to consider stopping when a person with type 2 diabetes is at risk of dehydration?
test.why: NICE NG28 rec 1.10.1: sick-day rules specify whether medicines should be stopped if there is a risk of dehydration, vomiting and diarrhoea, naming metformin and SGLT-2 inhibitors.

whyNot.0: Statins are not named in diabetes sick-day rules.
whyNot.2: Levothyroxine is not linked to dehydration risk here.
whyNot.3: Omeprazole is not part of these sick-day rules.

explain.body: Before starting, check for previous DKA, intercurrent illness, dehydration risk and ketogenic diets. Advise people to discuss very low-carbohydrate diets first, as the drug may need to be suspended.

items.label: check when unwell, whatever the glucose

test.q: A man on an SGLT-2 inhibitor plans to start a ketogenic diet. What does NICE advise?
options: Speak to his clinician before starting it
The diet is encouraged with these drugs
Double his dose for the first week
test.why: NICE NG28 rec 1.21.3: a very low-carbohydrate or ketogenic diet increases DKA risk; speak to a healthcare professional first, and the SGLT-2 inhibitor may need to be suspended.

whyNot.1: The diet raises DKA risk with these drugs.
whyNot.2: A higher dose would add to the risk.
whyNot.3: Changing the dosing schedule does not address DKA risk.

explain.body: On any admission and if status changes: shoes, socks, bandages and dressings off; examine both feet for neuropathy (10 g monofilament), ischaemia, ulcer, callus, infection, deformity, gangrene and Charcot.

test.q: Which instrument does NICE NG19 specify to test for neuropathy in the diabetic foot?
test.why: NICE NG19 rec 1.3.4: use a 10 g monofilament as part of a foot sensory examination.

whyNot.0: A tuning fork tests vibration but is not the NG19-specified tool.
whyNot.1: A neurotip tests sharp sensation but is not the NG19 tool.
whyNot.2: A tendon hammer tests reflexes, not the NG19 sensory screen.

explain.body: Limb- or life-threatening (ulcer with sepsis or ischaemia, deep infection, gangrene): refer immediately to acute services. Inpatients: MDT foot service within 24 hours of the first foot exam. Community active problems: within 1 working day.

test.q: A woman with diabetes has a black, dry toe (gangrene). How urgently should she be referred?
test.why: NICE NG19 rec 1.4.1: gangrene is a limb-threatening problem; refer immediately to acute services.

whyNot.0: 1 working day is for other active problems.
whyNot.2: 2–4 weeks is the foot protection service time for new high-risk referrals.
whyNot.3: Gangrene cannot wait for a routine review.
